Our Senior Pastor teaches that good works are not the means by which a believer is saved, but rather the proof and result of salvation [1][3].

She explains that good works serve as evidence of our salvation and a sign that we have received the divine nature of God [1]. Just as God Himself does good works, such as creating the heavens and the earth and declaring it "very good," so too when believers perform good works like forgiveness or generosity, they are proving they are like their Father [1]. God's nature is a giving nature, demonstrated by Him giving His only begotten Son (John 3:16) [1]. Therefore, when we are generous, we show that our nature has been changed [1].

Good works are not the price we pay to be saved [1]. Salvation is a gift from God, received by grace through faith, and not by works, so that no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [2][9][16]. Our Senior Pastor emphasizes that you don't pay for a gift; it is given freely, prompting celebration and rejoicing [9]. We are justified by His grace, meaning we can stand before God as if we never sinned [7]. Under the law, people did good works to be saved, accepted, or justified, but as new creations, we do good works *because* we are justified and God has already approved of us; it is our nature, not an attempt to earn His favor [3]. God does both the making and the saving, and there are no bragging rights for us [14].

Furthermore, good works are part of God's plan, predating our birth [4]. God pre-ordained us unto good works just as He pre-ordained us unto salvation [4]. He has prepared works for us to walk in from the foundation of the world (Ephesians 2:10) [2][4][9][16]. This means that salvation gives meaning and purpose to our lives; we are created in Christ Jesus to join Him in the work He does [14].

Our Senior Pastor clarifies that the good works God has ordained for us are primarily the "good works of ministry," not general acts like building roads or constructing houses [2]. The power of the Holy Spirit in a believer's life is given specifically for these good works of ministry, enabling us to be witnesses (Acts 1:8) [2][11]. God redeemed us so that we can join Jesus in this noble work, going about doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil, just as Jesus did (Acts 10:38) [14].

Yes, Dad often shares his experiences learning and serving in church, particularly with the keyboard.

Here's what he has taught across various messages:

*   In **Prayer Works**, Dad shared that one of the first things he did in his family church was to learn how to play the keyboard. He volunteered, saying he could play, and was given the opportunity. After they saw he played well, he joined the choir and eventually "displaced all the organist of the church because I was better than them," even as a GSS3 student. He attributes his advancement to giving himself to his own development and growth, which led the church to find him useful and an asset, progressing to playing at Lagos district and national levels [1]. He recalled making up his mind not to remain inferior and began to give himself to God's word, prayer, fasting, listening to the word, and evangelism, which enabled his growth and usefulness despite being young [2].
*   In **Faith and Healing**, Dad recounted trekking through certain areas about 28 years ago to get to church to serve and "to learn how to play the keyboard for church." He remembered confessing and meditating on the Word during those treks [6].
*   In **How GOD Calls and Why GOD Calls Into the Ministry**, Dad spoke about being a choir director in his fellowship and joyfully volunteering himself and their keyboard to play for meetings of another ministry's founder, hoping for an impartation, though he was not noticed at the time [3][14]. He questioned why great men of God weren't noticing his "great vision from heaven" [3].
*   In **How to Have a Great Year - Part 5**, Dad mentioned that God told him to serve. He would take his fellowship's keyboard and volunteer to play for other fellowships' meetings, even when he had no business being in school. He noted that the founder of those fellowships never noticed him, but the Lord told him he was there to serve the anointing, and that "the anointing knows who is serving it" [4].
*   In **The Sacrosanctity of GOD's Choice of Men 2**, Dad shared an experience years ago where he played keyboard, earning 3,000 naira monthly and a pair of black shoes at a church called Rema Chapel. He said that after hearing the word of God there and experiencing all-night prayer meetings, he knew it was his church and told the pastor not to pay him anymore, even though his previous church had the latest keyboard and this new church was dusty with basic equipment [5][9].

Here is what the messages cover regarding house churches:

*   **40 Dot Immersion** Dad teaches that the move of these last days is the move of the Saints, encouraging a "military mindset" for disciples. He describes how to start a house church, beginning by inviting people to a watch party, which then becomes a cell or house church. He emphasizes that a house church can start with just two people, like a husband and wife, because "when two or three are gathered," it is a gathering in God's eyes. He gives examples of how Bishop Dogg planted churches by talking to relatives and neighbors [1].
*   **HCM 2025** Dad explains that a house church can start as a "watch party" and grow to four, then five people. He says you don't need more than three people to start a church, and in fact, "two, you and the other person" is enough. He shares that he started Heritage of Faith Church by looking for converts and preaching together with them as they were being converted. He encourages those feeling lonely or missing home to "join" online sessions and then invite people to their house to listen to the Word of God together [4][16].
*   **Wonders of Personal Fellowship** Dad clarifies that joining a physical gathering online is not the same as an "online church." He states that the goal for members in diaspora is to grow to the point where they can start a house church. He reiterates that a house church can begin with two or three people, and that this is how churches started in the early days of the Apostles, often in people's houses. He emphasizes that you don't need money to pay rent for a hotel room to start a church [6].
*   **Day 40 - Morning Session** Dad encourages those in diaspora, particularly referencing churches in the UK, to meet in house churches. He urges members to check on their invited people and perfect transportation arrangements for them to join gatherings [13].

Dad teaches that tithing, or what we primarily refer to as "partnership offering" at Heritage of Faith Church, is a vital act of worship and commitment to God's work and the spread of the gospel [1][3][6].

While the term "tithe" traditionally refers to a 10% giving and Dad acknowledges its practice in the Old Testament, he emphasizes that for New Testament believers, a partnership offering is a percentage of your income that you choose to set aside to support the ministry [6]. He encourages believers to give at least 10%, suggesting that with the Holy Ghost, one should strive to do even more than Old Testament believers did [3][6]. However, the decision on the percentage is ultimately a personal one, made as an act of free will, as God does not force anyone to give [6].

Dad explains that giving is a spiritual and sacred act, not to be done thoughtlessly [15]. It demonstrates the state of your heart and your commitment to the work of God, the spread of the gospel, and your purpose in Christ Jesus [9][11]. He stresses that if money is not involved, commitment is not involved [1]. As it says in Luke 12:34, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also [11].

Regarding the value of giving, Dad teaches that God does not measure an offering by its absolute amount, but by what is *left* after the person gave [12]. Therefore, a smaller amount given faithfully, reflecting one's financial capacity, can be more significant than a large sum given from an abundance that costs the giver little [10][12]. He clarifies that giving should be "according to your capacity," and this faithfulness is what matters, not just the size of the offering [10].

Giving also serves as a principle of the Kingdom that grants God permission to transform insufficiency into more than sufficiency, leading to multiplication in all areas of your life [2]. It is important to practice generosity and expect returns from God, rather than from the people you give to [4]. Dad reminds us that generosity is not selective; truly generous people are generous everywhere, not just in church [16]. While giving to the poor (arms giving) is honored by God, it is distinct from the partnership giving that supports the gospel's spread [1].

Dad encourages believers to talk to God annually about their "giving profile," ensuring it is instructed by God and not pressured by man, as he believes pressuring people to give does not lead to their prosperity [14]. The church does not police giving, but encourages faithfulness [10].

To overcome fear and anxiety, you must first recognize that fear is a tormenting spirit and a form of bondage that paralyzes and hinders progress [3][6]. Dad teaches that God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of love, power, and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:6-7) [3]. He also explains that anxiety is a manifestation of fear, a disturbing and scary thought about tomorrow, and that it exposes areas of your life to the enemy [2][8][15].

Here’s how to deal with fear and anxiety:

1.  **Repent from Fear and Confront It** Dad emphasizes that fear is like cancer; it spreads and must be cut off immediately [10]. You can repent from fear, just as David did (Psalm 34) [10]. When fear confronts you, you must face it directly and say, "no more" [1][15]. In one instance, Dad shared a dream where he rebuked a fierce lion, and it "skimped away," symbolizing overcoming fear [1].
2.  **Understand Fear and Anxiety** Anxiety is worry about a negative outcome, and it can become a stronghold in your life, leading to a pattern of living [2][15]. Job, for example, exposed his children and estate to the enemy through his fear and anxiety (Job 3:25) [8]. Many fears, such as the fear of flying or of not finding a partner, often stem from a deeper fear, like the fear of death, and psychologists say many are irrational because they will never happen [13][16][18].
3.  **Fight with God's Word and the Blood of Jesus** When the devil tries to whip up things in your mind, especially battles against fear and anxiety, you cannot overcome your thoughts with your thoughts alone. You must open your mouth and say the right thing [4]. Dad teaches to plead the blood of Jesus and harass the devil back, declaring that "by the blood of the Everlasting Covenant my mind is thinking the right thing" [4]. You can also say with faith, "I will never lose my mind; my mind is sharp" [4].
4.  **Master Victory Over Fear** You can dedicate yourself to mastering victory over fear by gathering all teachings and scriptures that address it. Look up every reference in the Bible that says "fear not" and meditate on them, praying in the Holy Ghost [5]. Dad clarifies that while the exact phrase "fear not" doesn't appear 365 times, there are many references in different forms that speak against fear and how believers overcome it [5].
5.  **Leverage the Presence and Love of God** The antidote to fear is the presence and love of God [11][17]. Psalm 23:4 says, "Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me" [11]. God is with you as one who loves you, with good intentions to protect you [17]. When you understand that His presence means He is actively loving and protecting you, it drives away fear [11][17]. The love of God in your heart casts out all fear (1 John 4:18) [3].
6.  **Take No Thought (Don't Worry)** Jesus said to "take no thought," which means "don't worry about it" (Matthew 6:25-31) [2][8]. Worry is a disturbing, fearful thought about tomorrow [2]. Instead of staying awake worrying, you should cast your cares on God and let Him watch while you sleep (Psalm 121:4) [15].
7.  **Command Fear and Anxiety to Leave** Use your spiritual authority to address fear, anxiety, or any other oppression by name [7]. Dad instructs to use forceful language in the spirit, saying, "In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I command you... I overcome you. I come against you and I come after you by the power of the Holy Spirit. And I suppress you. I neutralize you now" [7].
8.  **Withdraw from Distractions** Sometimes, to overcome anxiety and fear, it's necessary to withdraw from distractions, including social media and people, as Jacob did for his breakthrough [9]. This helps you miss anxiety, fear, and the pressure of comparison [9].
9.  **Cultivate a Quiet Mind and Spirit** God quiets the noise of worry, anxiety, and fear in the mind [14]. The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Colossians 3:15, Philippians 4:6-7), will come into your heart and heal you from grief, ministering a quiet spirit which is of great price before God (1 Peter 3:4) [14].

Dad teaches that Romans 8:28 reveals a foundational truth for believers: "all things work together for good for them that love God and them that are called according to his purpose" [3][13][15].

This scripture highlights several key aspects of our walk with God. Firstly, Dad emphasizes that God is a partner in our labor, always the senior partner and the initiator in this divine partnership [1][13]. He will not join Himself to something someone else started; the partnership with God is possible only when He initiates it [1].

Furthermore, Dad clarifies that there is no such thing in scripture as "my own purpose for my life"; rather, what we find is "God's purpose for our lives" [3]. We are called according to His design and purpose [1], and there is a definite purpose and plan that God has for each of us [14]. This divine plan for our lives is revealed through His word and flows from His pure motives and deep love for us [15][18]. Therefore, we must consider God's plans and align our ways with His purpose, ensuring what we do does not contradict what God is doing [15][18].

The Holy Spirit plays a crucial role in seeing this truth manifest. Dad teaches that the Holy Spirit helps us to pray out God's will, and when prayer is done according to His will, God takes that prayer and works it out for our good in our lives [8]. Even in situations that may not feel good or seem like losses, Dad encourages giving thanks, because with God, "he works all things together for good" [11]. When we express gratitude, we begin to see how those things we thought did not work are actually fitting into God's greater plan, often leading to greater replacements [11].

Finally, Romans 8:28 serves as an example of a "certain knowing" or conviction that we possess as believers, standing in contrast to presumption [16]. It is a certainty that God is involved in our lives, and His covenant is working for us, even if we don't always feel it [1].

Dad teaches that Mark 11:23 highlights the profound power of speaking and believing God's word without doubt, emphasizing that faith is both a trust in God and an active force expressed through our words and actions.

He explains that faith is fundamentally about putting your absolute trust in God and His word [4][16]. It is believing and acting on what God says, because who you trust determines what you see coming in your life [3][13][16]. Dad emphasizes that God Himself is a "faith God," and living by faith is the way He expresses life, as well as the way we express eternal life [17]. This faith is not something we earn, but a gift already given to us and an eternal possession for those in Christ [17].

To turn your faith loose and set it in motion, Dad teaches that the primary way is by speaking [3][4]. Speaking is described as faith's most dominant, important, and initial act [2]. If you believe something, you must say it; faith has a voice, and without that voice, it is not truly faith [2]. This includes declaring what God has told you and saying of the Lord, "He is my refuge, He's my fortress, He is my God in whom I trust" (Psalm 91:2) [2][11]. Speaking God's word is essential for experiencing abundance and for seeing change and transformation in your life [4][7][12].

Beyond speaking, the second way to turn your faith loose is by giving corresponding action to what you are saying [3]. Dad gives the example of Sarah, who received strength to conceive even past age because she judged God faithful who had promised (Hebrews 11:11), demonstrating belief followed by action [3].

The concept of "not doubting in your heart" is addressed through the call for complete trust in God alone, not in yourself, other people, or even investments [13]. Dad highlights that true faith means doing what God has told you, regardless of how it might appear to others [15]. He cautions against using scripture to counter a direct instruction from God, stating that such an action would not be walking in faith [15]. Instead, we are to "put up our faith" daily, address specific situations with God's word, and trust Him for miracles [7].

In his message, "How to Build Lasting Relationships," Pastor Andrew Eluwa shared several other important principles for how believers should conduct themselves and interact with others, both within and outside the church.

Beyond being part of the solution, Pastor Andrew Eluwa emphasized the importance of **not acting in your own name** when addressing issues or serving in the church. He taught that when performing any task as a church member or worker, it should never be done in your own name [1][3]. If you have a valid point or concern, he advised against expressing it publicly in a way that could sow discord or demotivate others, such as writing about it in a group chat, even if it "looks meaningful" [3]. Instead, you should approach the leader or whoever is on the appropriate layer you have access to, ensuring your feedback is genuine [3]. He also counseled against using phrases like "My pastor said..." when conveying information that might sound like it's coming from you rather than the church, as leaders can find such communication uncomfortable. He encouraged adding wisdom to your faith and communication [13].

Pastor Andrew Eluwa also spoke about:
*   **Serving God, not man** He stressed that you come to serve God, not man, and that you should not allow someone's actions or inactions to deter you from your spiritual possession [11].
*   **Using your gifts and avoiding idleness** He warned that it would be a "disaster in faith" to come to church and hide your gift, drawing on the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30) [11][17]. He explained that the natural tendency is to lose what you don't use, noting that "whatever is not deliberately protected disintegrates" [11].
*   **Avoiding projection and speaking with grace** He taught that sometimes you might be the only one thinking what you're thinking, and people often project their own reality or thoughts onto others, using phrases like "they say, they say" when it's actually their own complaint [7][8]. He used the example of Jesus asking "Who do men say I am?" in Matthew 16, understanding that people project themselves onto others [7]. Consequently, he emphasized that our words should be "seasoned with grace" (Colossians 4:6), spoken deliberately so the recipient receives them with understanding [7]. He further clarified that "open rebuke" means honest feedback, not public shaming [18].
*   **Allowing time for relationships to process** He advised that to enjoy the fruit of friendship, partnership, and career, one must allow time to process themselves or the other person [6]. He noted that sometimes, people who offend you might not even be aware they did so [2].
*   **Not making your life a "prayer project"** He cautioned against turning your life into a continuous "prayer project," where you constantly seek out prophets and apostles for every issue, encouraging a focus on connecting with God instead [6].
*   **Mind what you say about others** He underscored the power of words, urging parents never to allow anyone to body shame their children, even jokingly [6]. Conversely, he also advised not paying attention to every remark made about you [16].
*   **Cultivating gratitude over entitlement** Pastor Andrew Eluwa distinguished between true entitlement and a "false entitlement mentality" which kills gratitude [12]. He encouraged expressing thanks even when you are meant to be entitled, as this is how mature individuals act [12]. He also linked stinginess or a reluctance to give to hindering financial or business breakthroughs for some Christians [12].
*   **Celebrating others' achievements** He strongly emphasized the importance of genuinely celebrating people's achievements and being happy for them, citing Romans 12:15 to "Rejoice with them that rejoice" [14][17]. He warned that if you cannot genuinely be happy for others, they will run away from you, and this is easily detectable [17]. He shared an illustration of two friends reacting differently to a new house, with one being genuinely happy and the other finding faults [14].
*   **God testing associations** He encouraged praying that God would test every association in your life, referencing the account of Gideon's army in Judges 7:3 where God "thinned out" the people to identify those truly committed [5][9][10]. He warned that people to be wary of in any relationship are those who have "nothing to lose," as they will depart at any slight discomfort [10]. This is because "where your heart is," your treasure is, and if there's no treasure, there's no stake [5][10].
*   **Holistic growth** Referencing Luke 2:52, which speaks of Jesus growing in stature, Pastor Andrew Eluwa spoke about the "four pillars of life," emphasizing the importance of taking care of your physical body through diet and exercise, as this body is needed to function in this realm [15].
*   **Discipline children directly** He also shared a practical example about handling children in your home, stating that if a guest's child is misbehaving or being overly indulgent, you should address it directly and not allow the child to go unchecked, even if the parent encourages it. This prevents projecting your own thoughts about the child onto them later [4].
*   **Managing access to successful friends** He noted that it would be foolish to treat a successful friend, such as a state governor, as if they are still just a "schoolmate" without managing access appropriately [18].

Dad teaches that he will never tell the church who you should vote for in any election, including the 2027 Nigerian elections, because it is a matter of personal conviction and not within his pastoral jurisdiction [6][11][13].

He emphasizes that your vote is your power and as a believer, you have a divine obligation to vote in elections [9]. If you are of voting age, you should get your Permanent Voter's Card (PVC) [4][8][9][18]. Dad encourages Christians to participate in the electoral processes and even to join political parties, stating that it is not a sin for a Christian to be in politics and that joining a party is more important than just voting [4][13][18]. This allows believers to "infiltrate into the system" and work towards change from within [4][13]. He advises thinking long-term about political ambitions, starting small, and patiently building up, rather than expecting to become a governor or president overnight [4][13].

When it comes to making your voting choice, Dad cautions against voting based on excitement for a candidate, unnecessary sentiments like gender, tribe, or religion, or being swayed by money or food [9][11]. Instead, you should evaluate candidates based on their intelligible and visible plans for Nigeria, focusing on who can truly get the job done [9]. He also advises supporting an ideology and making it a movement, rather than just focusing on one candidate for a single election [3].

Once a leader wins an election and is sworn into office, Dad teaches that they become a "minister of God" according to Romans 13:1, and all citizens, including Christians, come under their authority [6][16][18]. He strongly advises against speaking against them or cursing the country, but rather to bless Nigeria [15][16][18]. Instead of fighting with people online or physically over political choices, which can lead to losing covenant relationships, Dad instructs believers to pray for elected officials, recognizing that there are spiritual realities and demonic influences over regions that work against God's agenda [7][14]. He emphasizes that you should never put confidence in a politician, but in God alone [10]. Dad also warns against being a "toxic Christian" who cannot tolerate others' political leanings or call someone a devil for not supporting your candidate, saying that such behavior is like witchcraft [11].

Finally, Dad clarifies that the church is not a political party, and its assignment is not to build roads or perform other governmental functions [1][2][5]. He states that he will never give his microphone to a politician to speak to the congregation, unless they are an ordained minister, to prevent the church from becoming a political campaign ground and corrupting its calling [1].

Dad teaches extensively about money matters, emphasizing that finances are a spiritual issue requiring divine guidance and wise stewardship.

Here are some key insights from Dad's messages:

*   In **How to Have a Great Year (A Charge)**, Dad teaches that divine guidance in your finances is crucial, and if you master hearing God concerning money, you will master it for every other area of your life [1]. He reminds us that the love of money is the root of all evil (1 Timothy 6:10) and encourages asking God for direction in your giving, rather than blindly following others' percentages [1]. He also advises practicing "delayed spending" to allow time for thoughtful financial decisions, and notes that God always brings a supply whenever He speaks to you about a need, desiring you to have more than enough [1][10].
*   In **New Creation Realities**, Dad explains that the word of God teaches the proper attitude a Christian should have towards money, which is primarily one of stewardship. He emphasizes that money is not truly ours, but belongs to God, and we are merely in possession of it, accountable to Him [8].
*   In **Honour to Whom It Is Due Part IV**, Dad identifies saving money as a major mark of financial maturity, but stresses that the next, more important step is the ability to invest. He explains that money trapped is useless and depreciates; it needs to flow to multiply through right application. The main motivation for saving should be to put money to good use, saving for opportunities to invest that can change your life, rather than just for saving's sake [7].
*   In **No One Is Exempted - Giving Series Part 2**, Dad highlights the importance of being disciplined with money, especially for men, noting that good management of money provides a woman with a sense of security in a relationship. He suggests asking a potential spouse if they have savings, as this speaks a lot about their character beyond just money [18].
*   In **Wisdom for Godly Families - HOF Family Weekend 2025 Day 2**, Dad teaches that if you are a person of values, you will eventually have money, as money is exchanged for value. He warns against allowing dollar signs to control your life and reiterates that the love of money is the root of all evil (1 Timothy 6:10). Believers should be lovers of God and God's people, not lovers of money, the world, or the things in it (1 John 2:15-17) [14].
*   In **End of Month Fasting and Prayers**, Dad shares the wisdom of understanding the difference between what in a blessing is to be eaten for enjoyment and what is to be sown as a seed. He explains that God's blessings are designed for perpetuity, but they can stop if we fail to identify and sow the seed in every blessing to ensure its continuation, even beyond money to career advancement [9].

Our Senior Pastor teaches that salvation is a free gift received by grace through faith, not by good works. Instead, good works are the result and proof of salvation, flowing from the believer's new nature in Christ.

Our Senior Pastor emphasizes that salvation is a gift from God, given by His mercy and grace, not something that can be earned by human effort or good deeds [8][14]. She states that it is not according to works of righteousness that God saves us, but according to His mercy, which is the basis of all Jesus did in the work of redemption [14] (Titus 3:5-7). She warns against any teaching that suggests "Jesus plus something" is needed, as this distorts the gospel of Christ [8]. We are justified by His grace, allowing us to stand before Him as if we had never sinned [14]. Salvation is so profound that you cannot improve upon it once you are saved, nor can you improve upon the work of redemption, which is already done [9].

Instead of being the price for salvation, good works are the evidence or proof that we are saved [3]. They are a sign that we have received the divine nature of God, who Himself does good works [3]. Our Senior Pastor explains that when we forgive others, or are generous, we are demonstrating the nature of a giving God [3]. We do good works because we are justified, not to earn God's approval, but because He has already approved of us and we now have express permission to do His works [6]. Good works are the result of God working in the believer's heart, as people don't naturally do good; even moralists or atheists often have a self-serving reason for their actions [6] (Philippians 2:13, Hebrews 13:20-21).

Furthermore, our Senior Pastor teaches that believers are saved for a purpose, created in Christ Jesus unto good works that God has before ordained for us to walk in [7][11] (Ephesians 2:10). This means salvation comes with assignments. Part of these good works includes preaching the gospel, as every believer has been sent to do so [7][11]. Other examples of good works or divine assignments mentioned include parenting well and raising children, which she states is why nobody is permitted to be barren, as it would mean missing out on this good work [5].

Faith is essential for salvation and comes by hearing the Word of God [2][12][16] (Romans 10:17). Our Senior Pastor teaches that the gospel doesn't demand faith from us, but rather imparts faith to us [12]. God gave us His own faith to receive salvation [1][12]. This faith is not just for receiving, but also for doing and living, as the just shall live by faith [12][16] (Habakkuk 2:4, Hebrews 10:38). The Word of God acts as the vehicle that carries and conveys faith into the heart of man, and without it, faith cannot come, thus hindering salvation [12][16].

Our Senior Pastor teaches that discipleship is a structured followership of Jesus Christ that represents the glorious beginning of a believer's journey after salvation [1]. It is the process by which God molds and shapes us from our sinful, fleshly, and worldly ways into everything He desires us to be, a call to consecration that begins at salvation [4].

Discipleship is about "making" and transforming people, bringing out the "more" in a believer beyond their profession, qualifications, or skills [5]. It helps us to fulfill God's plan for our lives, which transcends our vocations [1][5]. While many are saved, our Senior Pastor emphasizes that without discipleship, the eternal life received may not visibly manifest, as it is the missing link for those struggling with old ways of living [15][16]. Through discipleship, we experience genuine conversion and the profound change and transformation God desires for us [15].

The local church is crucial to this process, as it is the place God designed for discipleship to happen, acting as a home where believers can grow, receive nourishment, and develop spiritually, just like a child grows within a family [1]. Our Senior Pastor highlights that discipleship aids spiritual growth by creating avenues and structures for development, such as small groups, teams for service, and sectors for soul-winning [12]. These structures are vital because spiritual things do not come naturally; the flesh often resists them [17]. The church provides accountability, ensuring believers develop essential spiritual practices like a consistent prayer life, which many would struggle to build alone [2][17].

Jesus taught His disciples fundamental truths, not just how to make money or excel in leadership, but things of higher priority like faith [3]. Our Senior Pastor explains that Jesus taught His disciples to pray [8] and demonstrated the power of faith, such as when He spoke to the fig tree (Mark 11:23) [3][11]. Discipleship also brings God's influence upon the believer through a closer walk and fellowship (Genesis 17:1), guiding us to choose God as our primary influencer in all aspects of life [13]. It introduces divine order, sometimes requiring us to leave familiar things behind to embrace God's plan, moving by conviction rather than sentiment, much like Abraham (Genesis 12:1-2) [9].

Furthermore, discipleship teaches us to "do the needful" in every situation and covers all aspects of life, including how to be an employer, an employee, handle business, and interact with people, emphasizing that a disciple's reputation matters (Titus 2:6) [7]. It is the solution for making the world a better place, given more discipled believers [7]. Our Senior Pastor teaches that discipleship also helps us deal with the old life, enabling us to walk in newness of life (2 Corinthians 5:17, Romans 6:4) because the power to say no to sin and live contrary to the old life has already been given to us (Romans 6:14) [14][16].

Ultimately, discipleship is also a call to faithfulness, where a disciple must learn and pass down exactly what they have been taught, without inserting personal opinions (2 Timothy 2:1-2) [6]. As disciples mature spiritually, they are expected to become disciplers themselves [10].

Dad teaches that while the church does not necessarily call it "tithe," they practice "partnership offering," which is a New Testament way of supporting God's work in the local church [3][6].

This partnership offering is distinct from "alms giving," which is the act of giving money to beggars or helping the poor; though God honors alms, it is not the same as supporting the spread of the gospel through the church [1]. Dad explains that giving is a powerful demonstration of a believer's commitment to the work of God and their purpose in Christ, emphasizing that where your money is involved, your heart is also involved (Luke 12:34) [1][9][11].

As a believer, you are encouraged to give where you are fed spiritually, and your local church is considered the primary place for your generosity to the Kingdom of God [3]. Regarding the amount, Dad encourages New Testament believers, who have the Holy Ghost, not to give less than 10% (the traditional tithe amount) and to consider giving more. He notes that your partnership offering could be a tithe of your income, 15%, or thereabouts [3][6][14].

Giving in the New Testament is an act of free will, not something God forces, nor should it be pressured by man [6][14]. Instead, Dad teaches that every year, you should talk to God about what He wants your giving profile to be [14]. God values offerings not by the absolute amount, but by the faithfulness of the giver, which means giving according to your financial capacity [10][12]. He illustrates that someone giving a large sum might be unfaithful if their capacity is much greater, while a smaller gift can be deeply faithful if it represents the giver's level [10]. The lesson from Jesus observing offerings is that God measures what is left after a person gives, valuing generosity that is commensurate with how He has blessed you [12][15].

Ultimately, Dad teaches that giving is a spiritual and sacred act that should be done thoughtfully and bountifully, reflecting your heart and commitment [11][15]. He also encourages a spirit of generosity that extends beyond church offerings to family and those outside the church, as true generosity is not selective [16].

I can only provide information based on the church's messages. From Dad's messages, faith is presented as a personal persuasion and a command for every believer, requiring active trust in God's will and consistent action on His Word.

Dad teaches that many Christians do not live by faith, even though they believe in God's ability [4]. The distinction between true faith and mere mental assent is crucial: mental assent may look and talk like faith, even mimicking its motions, but it ultimately fails to act on God's Word when faced with life's situations [2]. This often stems from a lack of attention, where focus is placed on personal needs and problems rather than on Christ and His Word [2][13]. True faith, however, is a personal persuasion and a decision to act on God's Word [3][6].

For a believer, living by faith is not a suggestion but a command [10]. Faith is never passive; it requires active resistance and doing something about challenges, just as David's household grew stronger [10] (2 Samuel 3:1). We are called to walk by faith and not by sight, meaning not by our natural senses, because anything beneath God's glory is depraved [7] (2 Corinthians 5:7, Romans 3:23). Dad emphasizes that God has given us faith, and we should live, talk, and walk by it, rejecting fear which God did not give us [7].

Every step we take should be a step of faith, a commitment in the direction God is leading, and every prayer we pray is a prayer of faith [1][3][5][8][11]. Dad teaches us to say, "No weapon formed against me shall prosper" and "If my God is for me, who can be against me?" as declarations of faith [1][3][5][8]. This faith is rooted in the knowledge of God's will—knowing not just that God *can* do something, but that He *will* do it because He wants to [4]. "Whatever it is that God can do, he will do it for me" [4].

We are to trust God with our entire lives, not man, our bosses, or our investments, but to have "Christ confidence" [17] (Jeremiah 17:5-6, Job 22:21). When challenges arise, we should view them as opportunities to act on God's Word [13]. Furthermore, Dad instructs us to say only what God tells us to say, even if it contradicts what a doctor or circumstances might present [10].

For those who are believers, Dad explains there is no such thing as "small faith" because the faith within us is the faith of God Himself [15] (Mark 11:22). This faith is activated and sustained through daily practices like reading the Bible, praying, spending alone time with the Lord, speaking God's Word in faith confession, and sitting under the ministration of God's Word [12][18]. He encourages us to give ourselves to God, as seen in examples like Moses and Jesus, for transformation [18].

Living by faith leads to a path of victory and prosperity, where "nothing is impossible with God," and all things are possible for the believer [9]. This process of transformation from consistently living by faith will "show" in our lives as sound health, healing, wholeness, fruit of the womb, character changes, and the complete disappearance of sinful habits and struggles [12].
